newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota president likes to tell it straight.
newsitem.headline: Toyota president likes to tell it straight.

text.p: It comes as little surprise to Japanese industry watchers that Hiroshi Okuda spoke up and set off a political storm in Britain.
Since taking over as Toyota Motor Corp's president nearly 18 months ago, Okuda has emerged as one of Japan's most forthright and innovative captains of industry.
In a country where tradition is prized, Toyota insiders say Okuda's constant advice to his managers has been: "Don't be afraid to change things. It's bad not to change things."
Under his leadership, the sprawling car giant has decided to introduce a system of promotion based on merit rather than age and simplified its management structure.
When he took over in August 1995, Okuda, now 64, became the first person outside the founding Toyoda family to get the top job in 28 years.
His vow was to make Toyota into a "young, flexible and active" company.

That included speaking out, as he did on Wednesday when he sounded a warning to Britain that if it was outside the European Monetary Union then Toyota might have to look elsewhere in Europe to base its future plants.
Okuda started work at Toyota in 1955, first in sales and gradually acquired experience in most key parts of the company, including finance and parts' procurement.

He took the helm at a difficult time for Toyota. It had been hit hard in its home market by stiff competition, including soaring imports, and in foreign markets by the surge of the yen, which had cut exports.
Eighteen months later Okuda can back up his words with success.
Last November, Toyota forecast parent company sales of 8.8 trillion yen ($72.1 billion) for this fiscal year to March 31, up from 7.96 trillion yen ($65.2 billion) a year earlier.
On Thursday Toyota's share price stood at 3,150 yen against 1,900 yen when he took over in August 1995.
Okuda has concentrated on three areas: Improving Toyota's product line-up, recovering domestic market share and developing overseas business.
Financial analysts credit him with success in all three as well as with breathing new energy into the company.
They say that right from the moment he took over, Okuda told it like it was and did not duck such questions as who gets on in a family-run business like Toyota.
He said he would respect the family but personnel appointments should be made on the basis of equality.
Insiders say Okuda's way of telling it straight has gone all the way down the line of what was once a conservative hidebound company.
"All the top people in Toyota now speak more freely," one car analyst said.
Okuda, taller than most Japanese, is a top-ranked black belt in judo who is far more at ease with foreigners and the media than nearly all other top Japanese businessmen.
"He's a really straight-talking guy, almost too upfront for some Japanese," the car analyst said. ($1=122 yen)
